title: The Document
The Document
text:
Advisor-Ready, Week 12
This is the term most likely to be misread, so here is the standard plainly.
Advisor-ready does not mean finished, polished, or free of problems. It means a reader who is not you can follow the argument from question to method without you sitting beside them explaining what a section was supposed to say.
A draft is advisor-ready when:

every required section exists in some form, with no placeholder headings standing in for unwritten content;
the research question appears in the introduction, stated directly;
the literature review is organized around themes and supports the specific opening your question addresses;
the methods would let a reader judge whether the question can actually be answered;
figures, tables, and captions appropriate to the project are present, and each caption stands on its own;
the abstract is drafted; and
references are complete and Zotero-generated.

The Monday assembly and whole-document exchange test exactly this: whether the document reads without the writer explaining the missing connections. Do not send the advisor-ready version until the Week 12 release screen is complete.
Also bring a short conversation brief naming the document’s central argument, its strongest section, its most serious remaining problem, and your questions for me. Naming your own worst problem is not a confession. It is the fastest way to spend the twenty minutes well.

Whole-Document Review and Revision Memo
Before the release screen, exchange the complete draft with a peer. This is an integration check, not a third graded peer review. The reader traces one chain through the whole document:

What is the research question and why does it matter?
What does the literature establish, complicate, or leave unresolved?
How does the proposed method answer that exact question?
What outcomes would be distinguishable using that method?
What limits, feasibility constraints, or program requirements remain?

The writer submits a one-page revision memo naming the three most important changes made after that review, the evidence in the draft that prompted each change, and any issue that still requires expert judgment.


Week 12 Release Screen
Submit the advisor-ready document by Monday, Nov 23. The instructor uses the core rubric below for a bounded readiness screen during Week 12. Complete the required release revisions and send the document to the Primary Advisor and/or Proposal Committee no later than Wednesday, Nov 25. The Week 13 conversation continues the critique while the professional review is underway.

text:
Core Proposal and Thesis Rubric
Program-specific requirements may add criteria. They do not replace these course-level standards.



Table 2: Core final-document rubric.









Dimension
Satisfactory evidence




Question and significance
The research question is direct, bounded, and answerable; the document explains why the answer matters in its disciplinary context.


Literature synthesis and source use
Sources are relevant and traceable; the review organizes evidence around patterns, disagreements, limitations, and the opening for the project rather than one source at a time.


Question-method alignment
The unit or cases, evidence or data, collection or measurement, and analysis address the stated question. A reader can judge what the design can and cannot establish.


Feasibility, ethics, and alternatives
Applicable access, timing, equipment, permissions, safety, cost, ethics, and approval constraints are named. The document includes a defensible alternative for the largest design risk.


Expected or actual outcome logic
A proposal distinguishes plausible outcomes and explains what each would mean without inventing data. A thesis keeps claims within the actual results and analysis.


Limitations and calibrated claims
Consequential claims are supported and no stronger than their evidence. Important limits and unresolved decisions are visible.


Reader-facing structure
Sections form one argument from question through significance; transitions, headings, figures, tables, captions, and abstract help a reader follow it without the writer present.


Disciplinary and program fit
The document follows applicable disciplinary conventions and includes a completed requirements crosswalk confirmed with the Primary Advisor.


Accessibility and references
The document is readable in its submitted format; figures and tables have descriptive captions and non-color cues; citations and references are complete and consistent.






Every dimension must be satisfactory for milestone 15. A dimension rated not yet satisfactory is returned with the specific missing evidence and may be revised under the course resubmission policy when the institutional deadline allows it.

title: Progress Reports
text:
The Template
Every report answers the same four questions. Keep it to one page. This is not an essay, and length is not the point.
1. What did you accomplish since the last report?
Be specific. Dates, meetings, hours, sources added, words drafted, analyses run. “I worked on my literature review” tells me nothing. “I added nine sources to Zotero, read four of them closely, and drafted two paragraphs on the nitrogen-timing disagreement” tells me where you are.
2. What did you struggle with, and how did you try to resolve it?
The second half of that question matters as much as the first. Naming an obstacle is useful. Naming what you already tried tells me whether you need a different approach or just more time, and it keeps me from suggesting the thing you did last Tuesday.
3. What is your plan for the next period?
Specific tasks with specific deadlines. “Keep reading” is not a plan. “Finish the three forward-citation papers by Oct 12 and draft the methods paragraph by Oct 15” is a plan, and it gives us something to check against next time.
4. What questions do you have for me?
Bring them written down. The questions you think of in the moment are rarely the ones that have been slowing you down for two weeks.

title: Progress Reports
text:
What “Satisfactory” Means
Progress reports are a completion check-in. I read them; I do not give line-level feedback on them. See the feedback tiers.
A report is satisfactory when it:

answers all four questions;
is specific enough that someone could act on it, with named tasks, sources, dates, or obstacles rather than general statements of effort;
is submitted before the deadline, which for meeting weeks means before your meeting time, not after it; and
describes the work honestly, including the parts that did not go well.

A report is not yet satisfactory when it is missing a question, is written at a level of generality that could describe any student in any week, or arrives after the meeting it was supposed to structure.






NoteA Report Saying “I Am Stuck” Is Satisfactory



Satisfactory describes the report, not the project. A week where you accomplished little, struggled with something you could not resolve, and have questions you cannot answer yourself is a completely normal week in thesis work. Write that down without dressing it up and the report is satisfactory. What is not satisfactory is concealing it, because then I cannot help and we both discover the problem in November.

title: Reading Protocol
text: Use this as a starting procedure when the course puts an empirical research paper in front of you. Keep it with your drafts and mark up the article in a format you can use. The procedure is a heuristic, not a universal map. Some disciplines use recognizable introduction, methods, results, and discussion sections. Others organize questions, arguments, observations, themes, cases, or models differently.

title: Reading Protocol
section: Do Not Read It Front to Back
text:
Do Not Read It Front to Back
The first instinct may be to start at the first word and read to the last one. For many empirical papers, a targeted first pass makes the structure visible before you read closely.
Read in this order instead.



Table 1: Reading order for a first pass through a research article.










Order
Where you go
What you are after




1
Title and abstract
The claim, in the authors’ most confident phrasing


2
Last paragraph of the introduction
The actual question, and usually the hypothesis


3
Results, findings, evidence displays, or key passages
The evidence connected to the claim


4
First and last paragraphs of the discussion
What the authors say the evidence means


5
Methods
How the evidence was produced, read only as closely as you need


6
The rest, if you still need it
Detail






The time required depends on the paper, the discipline, and your purpose. A targeted pass helps you decide where closer reading is needed.

title: Reading Protocol
text:
The Four Questions
For any paper, on any pass, you are answering these. Write the answers in the margins.

What question were the authors trying to answer? State it as a question, in your own words, in one sentence.
What did they conclude? Find the sentence in the paper that says it. Underline it. Do not paraphrase yet.
What evidence is that conclusion resting on? Point at the specific result, observation, estimate, figure, table, quotation, theme, case, model, passage, or other form of evidence. If you cannot find one, that is a finding.
Where are the seams? Mark where each section starts and name the job it is doing.

Question 3 is where the most useful work begins. If the connection is not immediately visible, you have found something worth investigating, not made a mistake. Question 2 gives you the authors’ conclusion. Question 3 asks what is holding that conclusion up. Learning to trace the connection between the two is a skill, and each careful attempt strengthens it.

title: Reading Protocol
text:
What Each Section Is Doing
Many empirical research articles and proposals contain the parts below, even when the labels, order, or boundaries differ. Once you can see the work each part is doing, you can compare that structure with other disciplinary forms and with your own draft.



Table 2: What each section of a research article is doing.










Section
The job it does
What to look for




Abstract
Sells the paper in 250 words
The strongest version of the claim


Introduction
Narrows from a field to one unanswered question
Where the funnel lands, in the last paragraph


Literature review
Argues that a specific gap exists
Whether it synthesizes or just lists


Methods
Lets a stranger repeat the study
What was measured, on how many units, compared with what


Results or findings
Reports what was found, sometimes with interpretation
Results, observations, themes, estimates, uncertainty, and the evidence available for each claim


Discussion
Interprets, connects, and concedes
Where interpretation outruns the results


Conclusion
Says what it adds and what comes next
Whether the claim has quietly grown


References
Shows whose conversation this is
Names that keep recurring






Two of these are worth flagging now. Results and discussion are different jobs, even when a discipline combines them in one section. Watch how the authors move from reporting evidence to interpreting it. You will need to make that move visible in your own work later in the semester.

title: Reading Protocol
text:
The Second Pass
Everything above is structural. It tells you what a paper says. It does not tell you whether to believe it.
The evaluative pass comes in Week 6, where you take each claim and ask how many were studied, how large the effect was, and what the figures are not showing. Do not try to run both passes at once early in the semester. Find the parts first. Judge them second.

title: Reading Protocol
text:
Common Traps

Looking up every unfamiliar term. On a first pass, keep going. Circle the terms and come back. Stopping at each one means you never see the shape.
Trusting the abstract. The abstract is the most confident and least qualified text in the paper. Check it against the results.
Reading the methods first and getting stuck. Methods sections are dense by design. They are step 5 for a reason.
Taking notes instead of marking up. Notes drift into summary. Marking up keeps you anchored to what the paper actually says.
Treating a paper as settled. A published paper is one contribution to an argument that is still running, not the final word on it.

title: Reading Protocol
section: When You Read for Your Own Project
text:
When You Read for Your Own Project
Add one question to the four above: what does this change about my question? Record the answer in your source notes while it is fresh. That running record is what makes the synthesis matrix in Week 8 possible, and it is part of your process portfolio.

title: Syllabus: CFAN 3091V
text:
Course Description
You have a great research idea, now what? How do you turn your idea into a proposal? It has been said, paraphrasing Edison, that innovation is one percent inspiration, 99 percent perspiration. In this course, we will start with an inspiring idea and sweat our way to develop a research proposal.
Most students follow the Proposal Development Track and develop an original thesis proposal. Students graduating in Fall 2026 follow the accelerated Fall Graduation Thesis Completion Track and apply the same workshops to a complete honors thesis. You will learn to identify a research question, navigate University resources, write in the conventions of scientific communication, design or evaluate appropriate research methods, and produce the complete document required by your track.
Students will follow a step-by-step process that starts with choosing and defining a research idea, then proceeds through literature review and the development of a hypothesis, aims, objectives, and a research strategy. The course provides tools for understanding the structure of scientific reports and proposals, literature searches, and basic data interpretation. Students will learn about different research approaches and how to achieve consistency in their research projects. The course guides students in beginning and developing a written research proposal that will satisfy the requirements of their advisors, institution, and funding organizations.
The course is designed for students across all departments in CFANS. Whether your thesis involves field experiments in agronomy, sensory evaluation in food science, econometric models in applied economics, or qualitative interviews in natural resource management, the research process and writing skills taught here apply to your work.
This is a writing-intensive, workshop-style course. You will write every week. Your writing will improve through practice, feedback, and revision, not through a single high-stakes assignment at the end. The final Full Thesis Proposal or Final Thesis Draft is the culmination of a semester of scaffolded writing practice.

title: Syllabus: CFAN 3091V
text:
How This Class Runs
We work mainly at the board and on paper. I do not teach from slide decks. Instead, we build questions, arguments, outlines, and revisions together while the decisions are still visible. Bring paper and something to write with to every session, along with any handout or draft listed for that week.
That choice is deliberate. A finished presentation can hide the choices, false starts, and revisions that produced it. Here, we will make those moves visible: test an idea, notice where it fails, revise it, and explain why the revision is stronger. You will practice the same process in your own proposal work.
The board work is one part of the course record, not the whole of it. The course site provides the schedule, assignment criteria, readings, and materials you need to prepare and follow through. Canvas is reserved for assignment submission, grades, private feedback, and student records. If you need course materials in another format, contact me early so we can make a workable plan.
Week 4 is the exception. We work on screens that week, because library databases and Zotero are the subject of the lesson and the work requires live access. Bring a laptop for both sessions. You will build and document a search: record the terms you tried, what did not work, what you changed, and why you kept particular sources.

text:
Specifications Grading
This course uses specifications grading within the required A-F framework. The grade is determined by which bundle of milestones a student completes at a satisfactory standard, not by percentage weights. There are no points, no curve, and no percentage weights.
“Satisfactory” means the work contains every required part and meets the observable criteria on the relevant assignment page. Time spent or effort claimed does not substitute for those criteria. Instructor feedback on drafts is intended to support development and revision.



Table 2: Specifications-grading bundles.









Grade
Requirements




A
Complete all milestones at a satisfactory standard; earn a “strong” instructor-conversation rating; and submit a complete process portfolio


B
Complete all milestones at a satisfactory standard; earn a “satisfactory” instructor-conversation rating; and submit a substantially complete process portfolio


C
Complete at least 80 percent of milestones, meaning 12 of 15, at a satisfactory standard; satisfy the three essential document milestones; and submit a partially complete process portfolio


D
Complete at least 60 percent of milestones, meaning 9 of 15, at a satisfactory standard, including the three essential document milestones


F
Complete fewer than 60 percent of milestones, meaning fewer than 9 of 15, at a satisfactory standard






There are 15 milestones, one for each week of the term. Each course track has an equivalent 15-milestone sequence on the course schedule and assignments page. When a milestone has several parts, every part must be satisfactory for it to count. The process portfolio is named separately in the bundles above and is not among the 15.
Three milestones are essential for every passing grade: the Week 12 advisor-ready document and release screen, the Week 13 instructor conversation and professional-review submission, and the Week 15 final document. Milestone counts create room for an imperfect semester. They do not create a path around the complete proposal or thesis that the course exists to produce.

How the Week 13 Conversation Is Counted
The Week 13 conversation appears twice in the grading scheme. The two uses measure different things, and it is worth being explicit about which is which.
As milestone 13, it asks whether you did the work. You arrived with the advisor-ready document, you engaged with questions about design and evidence, and you completed the release revisions before sending the document to your Primary Advisor and/or Proposal Committee. Coming prepared and finishing those revisions satisfies milestone 13.
As a rating, it asks how the conversation itself went, judged strong, satisfactory, or needs development against the criteria on the Week 13 page. The rating is what separates the A and B bundles.
A rating of “needs development” does not by itself cost you milestone 13. Like any milestone rated not yet satisfactory, the rating can be re-earned: schedule a follow-up conversation within one week.


What Counts as a Complete Portfolio
The process portfolio has four phase sections, a mentor interaction log, and a final reflection. The bundles above use these three standards.



Table 3: Portfolio completeness standards used by the grading bundles.









Standard
Requirement




Complete
All four phase sections, the mentor interaction log, and the final reflection. Every artifact listed for a phase is present, and each phase explains at least one consequential decision.


Substantially complete
All four phase sections and the final reflection, with no more than two listed artifacts missing across the whole portfolio.


Partially complete
At least three of the four phase sections and the final reflection.






The course assigns straight A, B, C, D, or F grades. Plus and minus modifiers are not used.
The scaffolded assignment structure, regular progress reports, and three rounds of individual meetings exist to get you there. To support that, I offer Study Hall Hours, by appointment, where we review current assignments, work through writing and research questions, and take on common problems together.


How Much Feedback Each Submission Gets
Not everything you submit carries the same weight of instructor response.



Table 4: Feedback tiers by submission type.










Tier
Work
What you get back




Completion check-in
Progress reports, primary-advisor identification, Professional Review Plan
I read them. No line-level feedback.


Scaffolded short writing
Writing Exercise 1, Method and Feasibility Blueprint
Brief feedback aimed at your next draft.


Substantive draft
Literature Synthesis Draft, Introduction, Literature Review, and Methods Draft
Detailed written feedback returned within seven calendar days and before the next dependent revision deadline. The Literature Synthesis Draft is returned by Nov 4; the Introduction, Literature Review, and Methods Draft is returned by Nov 18.


Student peer review
Peer Reviews 1 and 2
Assessed on the quality and specificity of the feedback you give, not the polish of what you submit.


Professional review
Primary Advisor and/or Proposal Committee Review and Response
Assessed on preparation, communication, and use of feedback.


Final document
Full Thesis Proposal or Final Thesis Draft
Evaluated against the criteria for the student’s course track and applicable program requirements.








Progress Reports
Progress reports are the backbone of the early course. Proposal Development students submit Progress Reports 1, 2, and 3. Fall Graduation students submit two thesis progress reports. Reports connected to Weeks 3 and 7 serve as individual-meeting agendas. This is the same structure I use with my graduate students. You do not show up to a meeting empty-handed.
Each progress report uses a structured template:

What did you accomplish since the last report? Be specific: dates, meetings, hours.
What did you struggle with? How did you try to resolve it?
What is your plan for the next period? Name specific tasks and deadlines.
What questions do you have for me?

Progress means different things at different points in the semester. Early on it might mean identifying your domain and contacting potential mentors. Late in the semester it means drafting and revising thesis sections.
The Progress Reports page carries the full template, what counts as satisfactory at each stage, and the Professional Review Plan.


Writing Assignments
Writing assignments build progressively. Early ones are low-stakes exercises; later ones are thesis section drafts. Each includes specific criteria tied to that module’s objectives. Written feedback is provided on all of them.


Peer Reviews
There are two structured student peer review sessions, in Weeks 9 and 11. You review classmates’ writing using a structured protocol with specific criteria for each thesis section. Peer review is a core component of this course: structured feedback from a different reader catches what you cannot see in your own draft.


Professional Review
Week 14 is a professional review, not a third student peer review. Students send the released complete document to the Primary Advisor and/or Proposal Committee by Nov 25, after the Week 12 release screen and before the Week 13 instructor conversation. The reviewers should already have reserved the review window and should plan to return feedback around Dec 9. Students submit review evidence, a response memo, and a prioritized revision plan. The grade reflects preparation, communication, and use of feedback, not another person’s response speed.


Full Thesis Proposal (Course Assignment)
The Full Thesis Proposal is the substantial course document and the culmination of the semester’s work. It includes an abstract, introduction, literature review, methods, expected results, discussion/significance, conclusion, and references. It must meet both your department’s and the University Honors Program’s requirements.
Do not confuse this document with the UHP Thesis Proposal Form. The UHP form is a shorter administrative submission filed through the Honors Reporting Center. It asks for your thesis title, a brief prospectus, and your committee chair. It is not a substitute for the Full Thesis Proposal.
The Week 13 instructor conversation is about your developing Full Thesis Proposal or thesis; it is not the UHP filing deadline. For spring or summer graduates, the UHP Thesis Proposal Form is due December 1. Confirm the current date and any earlier department deadline with your advisor and departmental Honors Faculty Representative.


Final Thesis Draft (Fall Graduation Track)
Students graduating in Fall 2026 submit a complete thesis draft rather than a new proposal. They should already have filed the UHP Thesis Proposal Form, formed the Proposal Committee, and completed enough research to support thesis completion. Their final thesis and UHP Thesis Completion Form are due December 14, 2026. The Dec 16 course submission consists of the process portfolio and a record of the completion submission. Committee approval is due December 21 and remains an institutional decision rather than a course grade.


Resubmission
Any milestone rated “not yet satisfactory” may be revised and resubmitted once within one week. I will give you specific feedback on what needs to change.


Extra Credit
This course does not offer extra credit. Instead it is built with multiple pathways for improvement: low-stakes early writing that builds toward higher-stakes drafts, structured peer review that arrives before major submissions, progress reports that let you course-correct, and a resubmission policy on any milestone rated not yet satisfactory. The grading structure rewards consistency and growth rather than single high-stakes moments. You are never out of options.

To graduate with Latin Honors you must complete an honors thesis in your major department. Your thesis must:

Committee Composition
Your thesis committee has at least three members: a primary advisor and two readers. Two rules constrain who those people can be, and students routinely learn about the second one too late.

At least one member, though not necessarily your primary advisor, must be tenured or tenure-track faculty at the University of Minnesota.

Use of Generative AI
We do not use AI tools in this course. No assignment requires one, no assignment expects one, and you do not need one to do well here.
That is not a technophobic position. It is about what this particular course is for. You are learning to take a vague interest and turn it into a question someone could actually answer, then defend that reasoning in writing. The value is in the struggle: the stalled paragraph, the hypothesis that collapses when you try to state what varies against what, the draft you rewrite four times. A paragraph that arrives already smooth tells me nothing about where your thinking is stuck, which means I cannot help you. And you will be asked to defend this proposal to an advisor and a committee who will assume every sentence is yours.
What you submit must be your own thinking and your own words.
I may demonstrate an AI tool in class if it is useful to a point I am making. That is my call as the instructor, and a demonstration does not open the door to using one on your own work.
Honest representation of your sources, data, collaboration, writing, and tool use is required under the Student Conduct Code. If you are ever unsure whether something crosses a line, ask me before you submit, not after.

University Policies
The following statements are required by the University of Minnesota syllabus requirements.

Student Conduct Code
Students are expected to adhere to the Board of Regents Policy: Student Conduct Code. The University seeks an environment that promotes academic achievement and integrity, protects free inquiry, and serves the University’s educational mission. To support this environment, the University seeks a community that is free from violence, threats, and intimidation; that is respectful of the rights, opportunities, and welfare of students, faculty, staff, and guests; and that does not threaten the physical or mental health or safety of members of the University community.
The conduct code explicitly addresses disruptive classroom conduct, meaning behavior that substantially or repeatedly interrupts either the instructor’s ability to teach or a student’s ability to learn. The classroom extends to any setting where students work toward academic credit.


Use of Personal Electronic Devices
Classroom device policy falls under Teaching and Learning: Student Responsibilities. Using personal electronic devices in the classroom can hinder instruction and learning, for the student using the device and for others. The University establishes the right of each instructor to determine if and how personal electronic devices are used in the classroom.


Scholastic Dishonesty
Academic integrity standards are detailed in Teaching and Learning: Instructor and Unit Responsibilities. As students in a university community, you are expected to do your own academic work and to cite the sources of knowledge you draw on. Failing to do so is scholastic dishonesty, which includes plagiarism; cheating on assignments or examinations, including unauthorized use of online learning support and testing platforms; unauthorized collaboration, including posting student-generated coursework on platforms not approved for the course; taking, acquiring, or using course materials without faculty permission; submitting false or incomplete records of academic achievement; acting alone or with another to falsify records or dishonestly obtain grades, honors, awards, or professional endorsement; altering, forging, misrepresenting, or misusing a University academic record; or fabricating or falsifying data, research procedures, or data analysis.
When it is determined that a student has cheated, the student may be given an F for the course and may face additional sanctions from the University. The Office for Community Standards and the Center for Educational Innovation offer additional resources on academic integrity. Be wary of sites that advertise themselves as tutoring websites: it is not permissible to upload instructor materials to these sites without permission, or to copy material for your assignments from them. When you have questions, speak with or email me to clarify the practices expected in this course.


Excused Absences and Makeup Work
See Makeup Work for Legitimate Absences. Students will not be penalized for absence during the semester due to excused circumstances. Such circumstances include verified illness, participation in intercollegiate athletic events, subpoenas, jury duty, military service, bereavement, and religious observances. They do not include voting in local, state, or national elections.


Appropriate Use of Notes and Classroom Materials
Guidance is in Student Responsibilities. Taking notes is a means of recording information and, more importantly, of personally integrating and connecting it as part of your education. Broadly disseminating class notes beyond the current classroom community, or accepting compensation for taking and distributing them, undermines instructor interests in their intellectual work while not substantially furthering effective learning.


Grading and Transcripts
Grading policies and transcript regulations are defined in Grading and Transcripts.


Sexual Harassment, Sexual Assault, Stalking, and Relationship Violence
Policies are covered in the Sexual Misconduct Policy. The University prohibits sexual misconduct and encourages anyone experiencing it to access resources for personal support and reporting. If you want to speak confidentially with someone about an experience of sexual misconduct, contact a confidential resource on campus. If you wish to report sexual misconduct or have questions about the University’s policies and procedures, contact the campus Title IX office.
Instructors are required to share information they learn about possible sexual misconduct with the campus Title IX office. This allows a Title IX staff member to reach out to those who have experienced sexual misconduct to provide information about personal support resources and options for investigation. You may talk to me about concerns related to sexual misconduct, and I will provide support and keep what you share private to the extent possible given my University role.


Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Equal Opportunity
The University’s commitment is outlined in Board of Regents Policy: Equity, Diversity, Equal Opportunity, and Affirmative Action and Administrative Policy: Discrimination. The University provides equal access to and opportunity in its programs and facilities, without regard to race, color, creed, religion, national origin, gender, age, marital status, familial status, disability, public assistance status, membership or activity in a local commission created for the purpose of dealing with discrimination, veteran status, sexual orientation, gender identity, or gender expression.


Mental Health and Stress Management
Confidential support is available through Student Mental Health Services. As a student you may experience a range of issues that create barriers to learning, including strained relationships, increased anxiety, alcohol or drug problems, feeling down, difficulty concentrating, or lack of motivation. These concerns or stressful events may diminish academic performance and reduce your ability to participate in daily activities. University services are available to assist you. I care about your wellbeing; if health, safety, or mental health concerns are conveyed, I may consult with campus support offices to connect you with resources.


Academic Freedom and Responsibility
Academic freedom is a cornerstone of the University. Within the scope and content of the course as defined by the instructor, it includes the freedom to discuss relevant matters in the classroom and to conduct appropriate research. With that freedom comes responsibility. Students are encouraged to develop critical judgment and to engage in a sustained and independent search for truth. Students are free to take reasoned exception to the views offered in any course of study and to reserve judgment about matters of opinion, but they are responsible for learning the content of any course in which they are enrolled.
When conducting research, relevant institutional approvals must be obtained and the research must be consistent with University policy.
Reports of concerns about academic freedom are taken seriously. section: Monday: Research Paradigms: Quantitative, Qualitative, and Mixed Methods
text:
Monday: Research Paradigms: Quantitative, Qualitative, and Mixed Methods
Format: Focused instruction + question-classification workshop

Topics

Three ways of knowing: quantitative (how much? how many?), qualitative (how? why? what is the experience?), mixed methods (both, strategically)
When to use each: matching your question to your paradigm
Examples from CFAN disciplines:

Quantitative: yield trials, nutrient analysis, survey data
Qualitative: farmer decision-making, community food systems, lived experience
Mixed: adoption of cover crops (survey data + farmer interviews)

Common misconceptions: “qualitative isn’t rigorous” (it is), “quantitative is always better” (it isn’t)
Introduction to “statistical discernment”: we will go deeper in Week 6, but the core idea: you do not need to compute statistics to understand what they mean



Activity: Match the Question to the Approach
Most of Monday is this. I hand out a set of research questions drawn from across CFANS, on paper, with no labels. In pairs, sort them.

For each question, decide what the answer would have to look like. A number? A pattern across cases? An account of how something is experienced?
From that, name the paradigm the question requires.
Find the two questions you disagreed about most and write down why.
Rewrite one question so it would require the other paradigm. What had to change?

Step four is the one that teaches. A question is not quantitative or qualitative because of its topic. It is one or the other because of what would count as an answer.


Discussion

What paradigm feels right for your question? Why?
Can anyone give an example of a question that could be answered with either paradigm, and how the answer would be different?

title: Week 6: Statistical Discernment

Week 6: Statistical Discernment
text:
Monday: Reading Claims in Context
Statistical discernment begins before calculation. A result is interpretable only in relation to the question, design, population, measurement, and uncertainty that produced it.
That caution is not merely stylistic. In an introductory-statistics vignette experiment, both the wording of a finding and its topic affected students’ causal interpretations; using associational language by itself did not reliably prevent a causal reading (Hill et al. 2024). This study does not test our class activity, but it gives us a concrete reason to inspect the sentence and the study design together.

Reading Clinic: The Evaluative Pass
Fifteen minutes, on the Week 1 article, with the reading protocol in front of you.
Week 1 was a structural pass: what does this paper say, and where. This is the second pass the protocol promised. Take the conclusion you underlined in Week 1 and ask a harder question about it: how many of the seven inspection questions below can you actually answer from what the authors printed?
You will not answer all seven. The ones you cannot answer are the finding.


Claim-Inspection Protocol
For each result, ask:

What exactly is being claimed?
Who or what was studied?
What comparison produced the result?
What was measured, and how?
How much uncertainty surrounds the estimate?
Does the design support the conclusion?
Is the difference meaningful in the research context?



Guided Practice
The rest of Monday stays on the Week 1 article. You already know this paper, which means you can spend the hour on the inspection instead of on orientation.
I bring three claims about the Davis results and put them on the board. They are my sentences, not the authors’, and they do not all hold up. Your job is to run the seven questions on each one and decide what the printed results actually entitle that sentence to say. We work the first as a class, you work the second in pairs, and we compare answers on the third.
Expect to disagree about question seven. Whether an effect is large enough to matter is not a statistical question, and two people reading the same table can reasonably land in different places. That is the point of doing it out loud.

title: Week 6: Statistical Discernment
text:
Wednesday: Evidence Detectives
Bring two papers from your own field and audit them. You are not recomputing anything. You are working out what the authors are entitled to say.

What to Bring
Two papers, printed, that meet all of these:

primary research, not a review or a commentary;
reports numbers of some kind, whether means, counts, frequencies, scores, or participants;
includes at least one figure or table of results; and
close enough to your own question that you would consider citing it.

The numbers requirement is not a quantitative-only requirement. An interview study reports how many people were approached, how many participated, and how many raised a given theme. A sensory panel reports scores. Those are the numbers this audit is about.
Print them. You will be marking up displays and circling numbers, and the audit does not work if you are reading over someone’s shoulder at a laptop.


The Audit
Three questions do most of the work, and all three are answerable without software:

How many? Find the number, and find where it shrank. Studies report how many were enrolled, approached, or planted, then analyze a smaller number. The gap is where problems hide. Ask whether that final number supports a claim about a population, or only about the units actually measured. This question does not change between designs. A theme reported by three of 22 interviewees and written up as “participants described” has the same problem as a yield mean with four surviving plots.
How much? Find the size of the effect and its units, separately from any p-value. A yield difference of 0.2 Mg/ha can be highly significant with enough replication and still be too small for a grower to notice. Significance answers “is it real?” Effect size answers “does it matter?” You need both. Where the work is not reporting effects, ask the parallel question: how much of the evidence is this claim resting on?
What is the display not showing? A bar chart of means hides the spread. A table of percentages hides its denominator. A table of means hides the variation just as completely as the bar chart does. Look for whether you can see the variation, the individual observations, or the uncertainty. If you cannot, ask why not.



Group Report
Complete a claim worksheet for each paper, then report out on one of them:

the strongest conclusion the evidence supports;
one conclusion the evidence does not support;
how many units were actually analyzed, and what that limits the claim to;
whether the effect or pattern is large enough to matter in that research context;
what the figures and tables conceal about variation;
one design or measurement limitation;
one question you would ask the authors; and
whether and how you could use the result in a proposal.

The worksheet allows “not reported” and “cannot determine.” Use them. A question the paper does not let you answer is a finding about the paper, not a blank you failed to fill.
Across the room, expect at least one paper where the statistics are sound and the sentence describing them is not. That gap, between what was found and what was said, is the thing you are training to see. Expect at least one paper that says exactly what its evidence supports, too. Recognizing that is the same skill running in the other direction, and it is the reason this course is not teaching you to distrust everything you read.

Part 3: Taking One Paper Apart Together
Everyone works from the same paper. I will lead the dissection at the board, and we will complete the handout together. Keep the handout and your marked-up paper. They are the first entries in the claims-and-evidence record you will build across the course.






NoteReading for this session



Davis, A. S. (2010). Cover-crop roller-crimper contributes to weed management in no-till soybean. Weed Science, 58(3), 300-309. https://doi.org/10.1614/WS-D-09-00040.1


This is a guided structural pass, not a test and not yet a critical appraisal. We will work through four distinctions:

What is the paper about?
What question are the authors trying to answer?
What is one central claim the authors make?
What specific result, observation, figure, table, passage, or other evidence is connected to that claim?

We will record candidate answers, point to where they appear, and name what we are still uncertain about. “Candidate” matters. A first reading can produce a plausible interpretation that changes when we inspect the paper more closely.
The reading protocol gives you a starting procedure for empirical research articles. It is a heuristic, not a universal map. Different disciplines organize questions and evidence differently, and we will adapt the procedure as those differences appear.

section: Monday: From Source Notes to a Literature Structure
text:
Monday: From Source Notes to a Literature Structure
A literature review is not a sequence of article summaries. It is an argument about what is known, how it is known, where findings converge, and what remains uncertain.

Reading Clinic: Where Do These Papers Disagree?
Fifteen minutes to close the reading thread that started in Week 1. Bring the reading protocol and the Week 1 article alongside two sources from your own set.
Week 1 asked what one paper says. Week 4 asked where it got that. Week 6 asked whether it was entitled to say it. Today the unit changes: lay three papers side by side and find one place where they do not agree. A different finding, a different population, a different definition of the same term, a limitation one names and the others do not.
Disagreement is what the matrix below is built to hold. If three papers in your area agree about everything, you are either reading too narrowly or you have not read them closely enough.


Synthesis-Matrix Activity
After a short model, most of Monday is work time. Build the matrix in class so questions about categories, conflicting findings, and weak source notes can be resolved while the evidence is in front of you.
Start from the Week 5 Search Record. Before building the matrix, write a two-sentence source-set rationale: what question the set can answer, and what the search boundaries mean it cannot represent. Then create a working matrix with one row per retained source and columns for:

research question;
population or system;
method;
principal finding;
limitation;
relevance to your project; and
relationship to other sources.

Use the matrix to identify two or three themes that can organize your review.


Matrix Decision Rules
Use the same rules for every row:

Record the paper’s claim in language no stronger than its design permits.
Separate a different result from a different population, measure, definition, or method. Those are not interchangeable disagreements.
Mark “not reported” when the paper does not answer a matrix question. Do not infer an answer to make the row look complete.
Put sources in the same theme only when you can name the shared question or concept.
Treat a gap as bounded by the Search Record. “I did not find” is not the same claim as “no research exists.”

title: Week 8: Subject Mastery and Evidence Synthesis

text:
Wednesday, Oct 28: No Class, Independent Synthesis Work
We will not meet on Oct 28 because I am out of the office. The work does not disappear. Monday’s model, your synthesis matrix, and the paragraph shell below give you the structure for an independent drafting session.
Complete these steps:

Finish the source-set rationale and the matrix rows needed for the section you are drafting.
Draft one paragraph that states a pattern across multiple sources, identifies an important difference or limitation, explains why it matters for your question, and stays within the reviewed evidence.
Diagnose the paragraph yourself. Label the sentence that states the cross-source relationship, mark every sentence that discusses only one source, and identify the phrase that bounds the gap.
Revise the paragraph, then integrate it into the Literature Synthesis Draft. Save the original and revised versions for your process portfolio.
Submit the draft and its supporting Search Record and synthesis matrix by the Canvas deadline on Oct 28. Include one question you want the instructor or your Week 9 peer reviewer to address.


Paragraph Shell
Use this shell when the relationship among sources is still hard to state. Replace every bracketed prompt with language supported by the sources in front of you:

Across [source set], the evidence converges on [bounded pattern]. The sources differ in [finding, population, definition, measure, or method], with [source or group] showing [supported result] and [source or group] showing [supported contrast]. That difference matters for this project because [consequence for the question or design]. Within the limits of [search and source-set boundary], the unresolved issue is [bounded uncertainty], which this project addresses by [specific question or design move].

This is a structure for reasoning, not language to submit with prompts still in place. If the matrix does not support one of the sentences, narrow the sentence or return to the sources.

title: Week 11: Expected Results and Discussion
text:
By the end of this week, you should be able to:

distinguish expected results, which a proposal projects, from actual results, which a completed study reports;
write an expected results section that follows from your methods and literature rather than from what you hope to find;
draft a discussion connecting those expected findings to the literature and to their limitations; and
give substantive peer review on another writer’s methods and expected results.







ImportantKey Distinction



Previous semesters identified confusion between “expected results” (what you anticipate finding, based on logic and literature) and “actual results” (what you found, based on data). This module focuses exclusively on expected results: the kind you write for a proposal before data collection begins.

title: Week 11: Expected Results and Discussion
text:
Monday: Writing Expected Results
Format: Short instruction, then drafting at the board and on paper

Topics

What “expected results” means in a proposal: projecting plausible outcomes, not making things up
The logic chain: hypothesis → prediction → expected outcome
What outcomes does your literature review suggest are likely?
What patterns do similar studies report?
Plausible alternatives: Expected result A if hypothesis holds; expected result B if it does not
Tables of anticipated findings: what would the data look like?
Writing the discussion: connecting findings to existing literature, acknowledging limitations, articulating significance, identifying future directions



Activity: The Two-Outcome Table
Most of Monday is drafting. Work on paper, one sheet per outcome.

Write your hypothesis in one sentence.
Write the prediction that follows from it, in the units you would actually measure.
Draw the table or figure you would expect if the hypothesis holds. Axes, units, and rough magnitudes. It does not need to be neat.
Draw the second one: what the same table or figure looks like if the hypothesis does not hold.
Write one sentence for each explaining what a reader should conclude.

Then trade with a partner and answer one question about their pair of sketches: could you tell these two outcomes apart if you saw the real data? If not, the prediction is not yet specific enough to be worth testing.


Discussion

For your study, what would it mean if your hypothesis is wrong? Is that a useful result?
How do you write about expected results without sounding like you are fabricating data?

Monday: Figures, Tables, and Abstracts
Format: Short clinics + proposal assembly workshop

Topics

General principles: clarity, consistency, accuracy, simplicity
Figure types and when to use each:

Bar charts, scatter plots, box plots for quantitative data
Conceptual diagrams, flow charts for frameworks and processes
Maps for spatial research

Table structure: row headers, column headers, alignment, units, meaningful ordering
Writing figure legends: descriptive, self-contained, concise: a reader should understand the figure without reading the text
Common mistakes: 3D charts, rainbow color scales, missing units, unlabeled axes, chartjunk
Tools: R/ggplot2, Excel, BioRender (for conceptual diagrams), draw.io (for flowcharts)
Abstract structure: context → gap → objective → methods → expected contribution (250–300 words)



Examples
We will look at good and bad figures from published papers. What makes each effective or ineffective?


Assembly Begins Monday
The clinics are short on purpose. The second half of Monday starts the assembly: put your sections in order, read the seams between them, and list what is missing. Wednesday finishes that work and tests it on a partner.
Starting Monday matters because the gaps you find are usually not sentence problems. They are a missing method detail or a claim with no source behind it, and those take more than one session to close.

Format: Workshop
Submit the Advisor-ready Full Thesis Proposal before class on Monday, Nov 23. The exchange below is an informal whole-document critique, not one of the two graded student peer reviews. Trace the question, literature-based rationale, method, outcome or expected outcome, and claimed contribution through the entire document.
Test the figure or table and caption without relying on the surrounding prose.
Mark every missing connection, unsupported claim, unresolved feasibility issue, and unmet program requirement.
Write a one-page Whole-Document Revision Memo naming the highest-priority revisions and the evidence for each priority.
Complete the instructor release screen against the core final-document rubric.

Are axes labeled, units specified, legends included?

Criteria

text:
Monday: Technical Writing Fundamentals
Technical writing helps another reader inspect your reasoning. The goal is not to sound complicated. The goal is to make the relationship among the question, evidence, method, and conclusion visible.

Topic Funnel
You left Week 1 with a domain. Progress Report 1 asks for a research question. This drill covers that distance, at the board, in four steps.

Broad domain. Write the area you care about in one phrase.
Focused problem. Name one thing inside it that is unknown, contested, or going wrong.
Variable comparison. Name what you would compare against what.
Testable claim. Write one sentence that could turn out to be wrong.

We start on prompts I supply, in pairs, before anyone works on their own topic. Expect the first few attempts to stall at step three. That is the hard step: a domain becomes a question only when you can say what varies against what. A claim that cannot be wrong is not a hypothesis. It is a topic wearing a hypothesis costume.


Diagnostic Revision

Select one paragraph from the writing sample you brought.
Mark its main claim, evidence, and reasoning.
Identify vague terms, unsupported certainty, and unnecessary wording.
Revise the paragraph without changing its meaning.
Explain which revision most improved the paragraph and why.

title: Week 2: Technical Writing and Thesis Requirements
text:
Wednesday: Thesis Requirements
Proposal requirements vary across programs. You are responsible for finding the requirements that apply to your degree and confirming them with the appropriate program contact.
Start from the Honors Program’s own document: Honors Requirements, University Honors Program (PDF). The thesis sections cover committee composition, the three thesis plans, and the filing deadlines. Read them before class. Two rules catch people out: at least one committee member must be tenured or tenure-track at the University, and at least one must be affiliated with the department where the thesis is conducted. Those can be the same person, but often are not.

Requirements Audit
Keep two deliverables separate in your notes:

Full Thesis Proposal: the substantial document developed in this course.
UHP Thesis Proposal Form: the shorter administrative form containing the title, brief prospectus, and committee chair.

The UHP form is not a substitute for the Full Thesis Proposal. The University Honors Program sets a baseline, while your department may require additional sections, approvals, or an oral presentation. Confirm both sources before you set your timeline.

Locate the available proposal guidance for your program.
Record required sections, approvals, and deadlines.
Mark any requirement that is unclear or unavailable.
Identify the person who can resolve each open question.
Add the confirmed requirements to your working timeline.

Do not infer a requirement from another department’s materials. When the published guidance is unclear, ask.


Outreach Protocol
Week 1 gave you three names. Today you write to them.
Faculty read a great deal of email. A message asking “can I do research with you?” gives them nothing to answer, so it sits. A message that names their specific work and asks one specific question gets a reply. Three paragraphs, under 200 words:

Who you are. Name, major, year, and that you are developing an honors thesis proposal in CFAN 3091V this semester.
Why them. One recent paper, project, or course of theirs, and the connection to the focused problem you funneled on Monday. Use Experts@Minnesota (experts.umn.edu) and recent departmental publications to find it.
What you are asking for. A 20-minute conversation, with two or three times you are available.

Draft all three in class. Then trade with a partner and test one thing: could this message have been sent to any faculty member in the college? If yes, paragraph two is not doing its work.
Hold the drafts until your Week 3 meeting. We will review them together, and we will coordinate the list so that three of you do not independently write to the same person in the same week. Primary advisor identification is due in Week 4, which means the sending happens with time to spare, not the night before.

title: Week 4: Literature Search and Source Evaluation
text:
Wednesday: Literature Search Workshop
Format: Workshop

Reading Clinic: Who Does This Paper Cite?
Fifteen minutes to open the term’s reading thread again. Bring your marked-up Week 1 article and the reading protocol.
Week 1 asked what a paper says. Today asks where it got that. Turn to the introduction and mark, for two or three of its framing sentences, which reference each one leans on. Then look at the reference list and ask how you would have found those sources if you had started from nothing.
That is the move pearl growing automates. Doing it by hand once makes the rest of the afternoon make sense.


Activity: Pearl Growing
Keyword searching in a field you just entered returns four thousand results and no way to rank them. So we will not start with keywords. Pearl growing starts from one good source and grows outward along the citation network, which is how the literature is actually organized.

Find one review article published in 2020 or later in your problem area. This is your pearl.
Backward search. From its reference list, pull the five sources it leans on hardest. Look for the ones cited repeatedly, or cited in the framing sentences of the introduction.
Forward search. Open “Cited by” for that review in Google Scholar or Web of Science, and pull five papers published since it that both cite it and speak to your focused problem.
Add all 11 to Zotero, tagged pearl, backward, or forward.
Annotate 3 of them: What is the main finding? How does it relate to your question? What gap does it reveal?

If you cannot find a review article, that is a result, not a failure. Either your problem is narrower than you think and you should search one level up, or the area is new enough that no one has reviewed it yet, in which case start from the most-cited primary paper instead. Flag it and we will sort it out in the room.


Partner Check
Exchange your 3 annotated sources with a partner. Can they understand why you chose these sources and how they connect to your question?

What Is the Honors Thesis?
The University of Minnesota Honors Program requires students to complete a thesis as part of their honors requirements. The thesis:

Must be an original scholarly or creative work
Must be supervised by a UMN faculty member
Must be approved by the student’s honors committee
Requirements may vary by department: please check with your unit’s honors coordinator

The Honors Program’s own requirements document is posted here: Honors Requirements, University Honors Program (PDF).
Two committee rules are worth knowing before you agree to serve. The committee has at least three members, a primary advisor and two readers. At least one member must be tenured or tenure-track at the University, though not necessarily the primary advisor, and at least one member must be affiliated with the department in which the thesis is conducted. Non-tenure-track University instructors and researchers with relevant expertise may serve as readers; anyone outside the University requires a departmental petition approved by the Honors Program Director.

Milestone 4: Primary Advisor Identification
Week 4, due Wednesday, September 30.
This milestone asks you to name the faculty member who has agreed to serve as your Primary Advisor. The work leading to it is spread across three weeks: the Week 1 freewrite feeds the Week 2 topic funnel, you identify candidates and draft messages in Week 2, and we review and coordinate them at your Week 3 meeting before anything is sent.
That sequencing is deliberate. We coordinate the list so that three students do not independently write to the same person in the same week, and sending happens with time to spare rather than the night before.

What You Are Asking Someone To Do
Faculty say yes more readily when they know the size of the commitment. It is roughly seven touchpoints across the term, the largest being one 30-minute meeting in Weeks 2 to 4 and a document review around Dec 3 to 9. The full list is on the Advisor FAQ, which also contains a template letter you may send them.
Point them at that page. A request that comes with a clear scope is easier to accept than one that does not.


Satisfactory
The milestone is satisfied by naming a faculty member who has agreed, with:

their name, department, and the date they agreed;
how the agreement was made, meaning a meeting, an email reply, or a conversation you can point to; and
confirmation that they know the approximate December review window.



If No One Has Agreed by September 30
This is the one milestone that depends on whether another person replies to email, and a silent inbox is not a failure of your work. It is assessed on your professional communication, which is entirely within your control.
If no faculty member has agreed by Sep 30, submit instead:

the three messages you sent, with the dates you sent them;
at least one follow-up, sent no sooner than five business days after the original and no later than Sep 28;
any replies received, including declines; and
a short note on what you will try next, naming at least one further candidate.

That submission is satisfactory. Then come see me. A stalled advisor search is usually a targeting problem or a timing problem, and both are fixable, but only if I know about it in September rather than October.






ImportantDo Not Wait Until September 30 To Tell Me



If all three of your candidates have declined by the middle of Week 3, say so at your individual meeting. I can suggest faculty, and an introduction that comes from me lands differently than a cold email. The students who struggle here are not the ones whose first choices said no. They are the ones who waited.

section: Writing Exercise 1 and the Topic Funnel
text:
Writing Exercise 1 and the Topic Funnel
Week 2, completed in class. Two pieces, both submitted together.
The topic funnel takes your domain and narrows it in four steps: broad domain, focused problem, variable comparison, testable claim. We start on prompts I supply before anyone works on their own topic.
Expect to stall at step three. That is the hard step, and it is hard for everyone: a domain becomes a question only when you can say what varies against what. A claim that cannot turn out to be wrong is not a hypothesis. It is a topic wearing a hypothesis costume.
The diagnostic revision works on one paragraph from the writing sample you bring. Mark its claim, evidence, and reasoning. Find the vague terms, the unsupported certainty, and the words doing no work. Revise without changing the meaning. Then explain which change improved it most, and why.
Satisfactory means all four funnel steps attempted with a claim at step four that could be false, the paragraph revised, and the explanation naming a specific change rather than saying the writing is now clearer.

Apply both to the central argument of the thesis you are completing. Replace the outreach drafts with a Thesis Completion Plan naming missing sections, remaining research or analysis, department requirements, and dated actions through the UHP completion process.

Structure

title: Peer Review Guidelines
text:
General Guidelines

As a Reviewer

Read the full document before writing any comments
Start with what works: identify specific strengths before addressing weaknesses
Be specific: “This paragraph is unclear” is unhelpful. “The transition between your literature review and your research question on page 3 is abrupt: consider adding a sentence that connects Theme X to your specific gap” is actionable.
Ask questions: “What would happen if…?” and “Have you considered…?” are more productive than “This is wrong.”
Focus on the work, not the person: “The methods section needs more detail” not “You didn’t write enough.”



As a Receiver

Read all feedback before reacting: your first instinct may be defensive; that’s normal
Separate the signal from the noise: not every suggestion needs to be adopted, but every suggestion deserves consideration
Ask for clarification if a comment is unclear
Document your response: in your process portfolio, note what feedback you incorporated, what you declined, and why

title: Peer Review Guidelines
text:
Peer Review Worksheets
The stable worksheet criteria are published below and may also be distributed through Canvas in an accessible paper or digital format. Each review requires you to point to evidence in the draft, explain why the issue matters, and name a priority. Three comments without that reasoning are not automatically three actionable suggestions.



Table 1: Peer review sequence and focus.










Review
Week
Focus




#1
9
Literature synthesis or thesis literature review: claims, evidence, synthesis, and organization


#2
11
Methods and expected results, or methods and actual results for Fall Graduation students: design, coherence, and support







Peer Review 1: Literature Synthesis

State the writer’s research question and literature-based rationale in your own words. Mark where the draft made each one visible.
Identify one paragraph that synthesizes multiple sources. Name the sources and explain what relationship the paragraph establishes among them.
Identify one place that remains source-by-source summary, or explain why you found none.
Test one consequential claim against its cited evidence. Is the wording no stronger than the evidence warrants?
Identify a disagreement, limitation, or boundary the draft handles well and one that needs more work.
Recommend the single highest-priority structural revision. Point to the relevant passage and explain what the revision would improve.



Peer Review 2: Question, Method, and Outcomes

Trace the argument chain: research question, evidence-based opening, proposed method, expected or actual result logic, and significance. Mark the first place the chain breaks or becomes hard to follow.
Test whether the unit, population, system, cases, or materials match the question.
Identify one missing design or analysis detail that would keep a reviewer from judging feasibility or answerability.
Check the applicable constraints: access, time, equipment, permissions, ethics, sample or case availability, and an alternative if the preferred design fails.
For a proposal, test whether at least two plausible outcomes can be distinguished using the proposed evidence. For a completed thesis, test whether the claims remain within the actual results.
Recommend the single highest-priority revision. Point to the relevant passage and explain why it comes before sentence-level editing.

After each review, the writer adds a short response naming one structural revision they will make, one recommendation they need to investigate, and one recommendation they will modify or decline with a reason. This response enters the process portfolio.

title: Peer Review Guidelines
text:
How Peer Review Is Evaluated
You are evaluated on the quality of the reviews you give, not on how well your own work is received:

Satisfactory: Every worksheet question is answered with evidence from the draft. The review identifies strengths and weaknesses, distinguishes a high-priority structural revision from minor editing, and explains why its recommendations would improve the question-evidence-method argument.
Not Yet Satisfactory: The review is generic, incomplete, unsupported by passages in the draft, or supplies edits without explaining their priority or purpose. It may be revised and resubmitted within one week.

title: Peer Review Guidelines
text:
Professional Review in Week 14
After the Week 12 release screen, send the revised proposal or thesis to the Primary Advisor and/or Proposal Committee. The Week 14 submission contains:

evidence that the document was sent and reviewed;
the comments, annotated draft, or meeting notes produced through the review;
a response memo explaining which major recommendations you will accept, modify, or decline; and
a prioritized revision plan for the applicable final deadline: Dec 14 for Fall Graduation students and Dec 16 for Proposal Development students.

You are evaluated on how you prepare for, document, and use professional feedback. Your grade does not depend on the reviewer’s writing style or the amount of feedback supplied.
A dated send record, your own summary of the substantive feedback, and your response are sufficient evidence. Redact personal contact information and anything unrelated to the project. Raw email threads and unredacted reviewer comments are optional and are not expected.
